title: Chapter 71 — The Jeroboam’s Story
paragraphs: Ship and breeze blew on hand in hand; but the breeze was faster than the ship, and before long the Pequod began to rock.

Soon the spyglass showed from the stranger's boats and manned mastheads that she was a whale-ship. But she was so far to windward, and moving past so quickly, apparently on her way to some other ground, that the Pequod had no hope of reaching her. So the signal was hoisted to see what answer would come.

It should be said here that, like the vessels of navies, the ships of the American Whale Fleet each have a private signal; all these signals are collected in a book, with the names of the respective vessels attached, and every captain is provided with it. By this means the whale captains are able to recognize each other on the ocean, even at considerable distances and with no small ease.

The Pequod's signal was at last answered by the stranger's hoisting her own, which proved the ship to be the Jeroboam of Nantucket. Squaring her yards, she bore down, came up abeam under the Pequod's lee, and lowered a boat. It soon drew near; but as the side-ladder was being rigged by Starbuck's order to accommodate the visiting captain, the stranger in question waved his hand from his boat's stern to show that this was entirely unnecessary. It turned out that the Jeroboam had a malignant epidemic on board, and that Mayhew, her captain, was afraid of infecting the Pequod's company. For although he himself and his boat's crew remained uninfected, and although his ship was half a rifle-shot away, with an incorruptible sea and air rolling and flowing between, he nevertheless conscientiously kept to the timid quarantine of the land, and flatly refused to come into direct contact with the Pequod.

But this by no means prevented all communication. Keeping a gap of a few yards between itself and the ship, the Jeroboam's boat, by occasional use of its oars, managed to keep parallel to the Pequod as she heavily forged through the sea (for by this time it was blowing very fresh), with her main-topsail aback; though, indeed, at times the sudden onset of a large rolling wave would push the boat some way ahead, but it would soon be skillfully brought back to its proper position. Subject to this and other such interruptions now and then, a conversation was kept up between the two parties — though at intervals it was broken by still another interruption of a very different sort.

Pulling an oar in the Jeroboam's boat was a man of singular appearance, even in that wild whaling life where the whole is made up of nothing but remarkable individuals. He was a small, short, youngish man, sprinkled all over his face with freckles, and wearing an abundance of yellow hair. A long-skirted coat of cabalistic cut, of a faded walnut color, enveloped him; its overlapping sleeves were rolled up at his wrists. A deep, settled, fanatic delirium was in his eyes.

As soon as this figure had first been sighted, Stubb had exclaimed — "That's him! that's him! — the long-togged scaramouch the Town-Ho's company told us of!" Stubb was referring here to a strange story told about the Jeroboam, and a certain man among her crew, some time before, when the Pequod spoke the Town-Ho. According to this account, and what was learned afterward, it seemed that the scaramouch in question had gained a remarkable hold over almost everybody in the Jeroboam. His story was this:

He had originally been raised among the crazy society of Neskyeuna Shakers, where he had been a great prophet; in their cracked, secret meetings he had several times descended from heaven by way of a trap-door, announcing the speedy opening of the seventh vial, which he carried in his vest-pocket — but which, instead of containing gunpowder, was supposed to be charged with laudanum. A strange, apostolic whim having seized him, he had left Neskyeuna for Nantucket, where, with that cunning peculiar to craziness, he put on a steady, common-sense exterior and offered himself as a green-hand candidate for the Jeroboam's whaling voyage. They took him on; but the moment the ship was out of sight of land, his insanity broke out in a flood. He announced himself as the archangel Gabriel, and ordered the captain to jump overboard. He published his manifesto, in which he proclaimed himself the deliverer of the isles of the sea and vicar-general of all Oceanica. The unflinching earnestness with which he declared these things — the dark, daring play of his sleepless, excited imagination, and all the preternatural terrors of real delirium — combined to invest this Gabriel, in the minds of most of the ignorant crew, with an atmosphere of sacredness. Moreover, they were afraid of him. As such a man, however, was not of much practical use in the ship, especially as he refused to work except when he pleased, the unbelieving captain would gladly have been rid of him; but on learning that the captain intended to land him at the first convenient port, the archangel at once opened all his seals and vials — devoting the ship and all hands to unconditional damnation if this intention was carried out. So strongly did he work upon his disciples among the crew that at last they went to the captain in a body and told him that if Gabriel was sent from the ship, not a man of them would remain. He was therefore forced to give up his plan. Nor would they allow Gabriel to be mistreated in any way, whatever he might say or do; so that it came about that Gabriel had the complete freedom of the ship. The consequence of all this was that the archangel cared little or nothing for the captain and mates; and since the epidemic had broken out, he was more high-handed than ever, declaring that the plague, as he called it, was at his sole command, and that it would not be stopped except at his good pleasure. The sailors, mostly poor devils, cringed, and some of them fawned before him; following his instructions, they sometimes paid him personal homage, as to a god. Such things may seem incredible; but, however astonishing, they are true. Nor is the history of fanatics half so striking for the measureless self-deception of the fanatic himself as for his measureless power of deceiving and bedeviling so many others. But it is time to return to the Pequod.
"I'm not afraid of your epidemic, man," said Ahab from the bulwarks to Captain Mayhew, who stood in the boat's stern. "Come on board."
But now Gabriel started to his feet.
"Think, think of the fevers, yellow and bilious! Beware of the horrible plague!"
"Gabriel! Gabriel!" cried Captain Mayhew. "You must either —" But that instant a headlong wave shot the boat far ahead, and its noise drowned all speech.
"Have you seen the White Whale?" demanded Ahab, when the boat drifted back.
"Think, think of your whale-boat, stoven and sunk! Beware of the horrible tail!"

"I tell you again, Gabriel, that —" But once more the boat shot ahead as if fiends were dragging it. For some moments no one spoke, while a series of riotous waves rolled past — waves that, in one of the sea's occasional whims, were tumbling the boat rather than lifting it. Meanwhile the hoisted sperm whale's head was jolting about violently, and Gabriel could be seen eyeing it with rather more alarm than his archangel nature seemed to justify.

When this interlude was over, Captain Mayhew began a dark story about Moby Dick — not, however, without frequent interruptions from Gabriel whenever his name was mentioned, and from the crazy sea that seemed to be in league with him.

It seemed that the Jeroboam had not long left home when, on speaking a whale-ship, her people were reliably informed of the existence of Moby Dick and the havoc he had made. Greedily drinking in this news, Gabriel solemnly warned the captain against attacking the White Whale in case the monster should be seen; in his gibbering insanity he declared the White Whale to be no less a being than the Shaker God incarnate, the Shakers accepting the Bible. But when, a year or two afterward, Moby Dick was fairly sighted from the mastheads, Macey, the chief mate, burned with eagerness to encounter him; and the captain himself being not unwilling to give him the chance, despite all the archangel's denunciations and warnings, Macey succeeded in persuading five men to man his boat. With them he pushed off; and after much weary pulling, and many perilous, unsuccessful attacks, he at last succeeded in getting one iron fast. Meanwhile Gabriel, climbing to the main-royal masthead, was tossing one arm in frantic gestures and hurling forth prophecies of swift doom upon the sacrilegious attackers of his divinity. Now, while Macey the mate was standing up in his boat's bow, and with all the reckless energy of his tribe was venting his wild exclamations at the whale and trying to get a fair chance for his poised lance — look! a broad white shadow rose from the sea, and by its quick, fanning motion for the moment knocked the breath out of the oarsmen's bodies. The next instant the luckless mate, so full of furious life, was struck bodily into the air, and, making a long arc in his descent, fell into the sea about fifty yards away. Not a chip of the boat was harmed, nor a hair of any oarsman's head; but the mate sank forever.

It is worth adding here, in parentheses, that among the fatal accidents of the Sperm-Whale Fishery, this kind is perhaps nearly as common as any. Sometimes nothing is hurt except the man who is wiped out this way; more often the bow of the boat is knocked off, or the thigh-board where the headsman (the officer commanding the boat) stands is torn loose and goes along with the body. But strangest of all is the fact that more than once, when the body has been recovered, not a single mark of violence could be found on it — and yet the man was stone dead.

From the ship the whole disaster, including Macey's falling body, was clearly visible. With a piercing shriek — "The vial! the vial!" — Gabriel called the terrified crew off from any further pursuit of the whale. This terrible event gave the archangel still more influence, because his gullible disciples believed he had predicted this very thing, rather than having merely made a general prophecy, which anyone could have done, and so happened to hit one of the many targets its wide margin allowed. He became a nameless terror to the ship.

When Mayhew had finished his story, Ahab put such questions to him that the stranger captain could not help asking whether he intended to hunt the White Whale, if the opportunity came. To which Ahab answered — "Aye." Immediately, then, Gabriel once more started to his feet, glaring at the old man, and vehemently exclaimed, with downward-pointing finger — "Think, think of the blasphemer — dead, and down there! — beware of the blasphemer's end!"
Ahab stolidly turned aside, then said to Mayhew, "Captain, I have just remembered my letter-bag. There is a letter for one of your officers, if I'm not mistaken. Starbuck, look through the bag."

Every whale-ship carries out a good number of letters for various other ships, and whether they reach the people they are addressed to depends purely on the chance of meeting those ships somewhere in the four oceans. So most letters never arrive; and many are received only when they are two or three years old or more.

Soon Starbuck returned with a letter in his hand. It was badly creased, damp, and covered with a dull, spotted green mold from being kept in a dark locker in the cabin. Of such a letter, Death himself might well have been the postman.

"Can't you read it?" cried Ahab. "Give it to me, man. Aye, aye, it's but a dim scrawl — what's this?" As he was studying it out, Starbuck took a long cutting-spade pole, and with his knife slightly split the end, to insert the letter there, and in that way hand it to the boat without its having to come any closer to the ship.
Meanwhile, Ahab holding the letter, muttered, "Mr. Har — yes, Mr. Harry — a woman's handwriting — the man's wife, I'll wager — aye — Mr. Harry Macey, Ship Jeroboam — why, it's Macey, and he's dead!"
"Poor fellow! Poor fellow! And from his wife," sighed Mayhew. "But let me have it."
"No, keep it yourself," cried Gabriel to Ahab. "You are soon going that way."

"Curses strangle you!" yelled Ahab. "Captain Mayhew, stand by now to receive it." And taking the fatal letter from Starbuck's hands, he caught it in the slit of the pole and reached it out toward the boat. But as he did so, the oarsmen, expecting it, stopped rowing; the boat drifted a little toward the ship's stern; so that, as if by magic, the letter suddenly came level with Gabriel's eager hand. He clutched it in an instant, seized the boat-knife, and, impaling the letter on it, sent it, thus loaded, back into the ship. It fell at Ahab's feet. Then Gabriel shrieked out to his comrades to pull hard on their oars, and in that manner the mutinous boat rapidly shot away from the Pequod.
After this interlude, as the seamen went back to work on the whale's jacket, many strange things were hinted about this wild affair.
